#2044. FIFA presidency: Election date, candidates and Gianni Infantino’s re-election chances

By Axel Clody | 06 Nov 2026 14:05

The FIFA presidential election takes place in March next year and the activity behind the scenes is already busy.

Gianni Infantino, the current president, is seeking a fourth and final term. Under pressure from the controversy over his attempt to sell the commercial rights to the World Cup, he is expected to face competition from two names.

Gianni Infantino has a second challenger for the FIFA presidency ? Japan FA honorary president Kozo Tashima joins former Tottenham defender Ramon Vega in declaring his intention to run, with the vote set for 18 March 2027 in Rabat, Morocco. https://t.co/rTC9Y0T88S

The most recent to announce his intention to stand for football’s top job was Japan’s Kozo Tashima, honorary president of the Japan Football Association (JFA), which he led between 2016 and 2024.

The official, who has also been a member of FIFA’s technical council since 2015 and played football in the 1980s, stressed that he has the support of the JFA and that his experience at the head of the national federation will help him take on the challenge.

Before Tashima, former defender Ramon Vega, who played for Tottenham, Watford and Celtic, announced last month his own intention to stand for the FIFA presidency, with a platform of strengthening governance. Since retiring in 2004, he has worked in finance and asset management. In 2019, Vega tried to stand but failed to secure the minimum support from federations.

To be a candidate for the leadership of football’s governing body, the backing of five federations is required, something that Vega and Tashima still need to seek. The deadline for candidacies to be made official is 18 November.

In the middle of this year, behind the scenes, Infantino was negotiating the sale of 20% of the commercial rights to FIFA’s competitions, including the women’s and men’s World Cups, to private investors.

Among the possible interested parties was Jared Kushner, son-in-law of Donald Trump, the president of the United States, who has a strong relationship with the FIFA president, the man responsible for giving him a peace prize last year.

The plan, however, was revealed by the The Times, which prompted an immediate negative reaction from almost all of the continental confederations. UEFA (Europe), CONCACAF (North and Central America) and the AFC (Asia), as well as several FIFA executives and advisers, condemned the idea and forced Infantino to backtrack.

The European body in particular was the loudest critic of the Italian-Swiss executive, pushing for his resignation or removal and threatening a boycott of FIFA competitions, an idea that was later dropped.

With time, however, the pressure eased and the president, with the ‘machine on his side’ for re-election, made his move. Last month, the Asian Football Confederation renewed its alliance with Infantino and now supports his re-election, with Japan, through Kozo Tashima, the exception.

He already has the backing of the CAF (Africa) and CONMEBOL (South America), and nothing changed with a recent new scandal, in which the French newspaper Le Monde revealed that FIFA paid $4m (around £3m) in personal taxes for its president in 2024, 2025 and 2026.

The current president is the favourite to have his mandate extended until 2031. Gianni Infantino has been in office since 2016 and was re-elected in 2019 and 2023. In theory, he could not seek a fourth term, but because he initially took over after the resignation of Sepp Blatter, that was not considered an election.

There are 211 national associations affiliated to FIFA, with 55 of them from UEFA, 54 from the CAF, 46 from the AFC, 35 from CONCACAF, 11 from the OFC (Oceania) and 10 from CONMEBOL. Each has the right to one vote, which is secret.

If there is a candidate against Infantino, whoever receives more than 50% of the votes is elected. If there are three or more in the contest (as could happen with Tashima and Vega), two thirds of the votes are needed in the first round. If that figure is not reached, the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated until only two contenders remain, with the winner decided by simple majority.

The 2027 election will be held on 18 March at the 77th FIFA Congress in Rabat, the capital of Morocco.

#2041. Blackburn Rovers 0 – 0 West Ham United | Half time report

A cold crisp afternoon, perfect for football saw West Ham seemingly doing their best to get into their opponent’s half after the last three weeks’ slow, ponderous starts. The Hammers spent the early moments camped in Blackburn’s half, accompanied by the noise of 7000 visiting fans making Ewood Park sound more like London Stadium on a good day.

Most of West Ham’s early movement was through Mayers and Austbø down the left, the two combining well with the full back pushed right forward in an adventurous set up by Scott Parker.

However it was Blackburn who almost struck first thanks to an overlap down their right and a shot that looped agonisingly over Hermansens’ goal. Mayers responded by fizzing one cross just out of reach of Piroe -nil nil at 20 minutes.

Engels, Austbo and Mayers combined well as the Hammers attacked repeatedly down Blackburn’s left, Austbø impressing in place of Solomon. Half an hour gone and few scares for West Ham:  A more competitive, aggressive start than in recent weeks. Piroe had one ball played through but his lack of pace allowed defenders to crowd him out.

The half continued in the same vein, West Ham looking well capable of scoring with most of the attacking coming down the flanks, Mayers on the overlap giving Scott Parker a new dimension to his Hammers offensive work.

Worryingly, Engels went over on his ankle just on the stroke of half time –  the teams went in at 0 – 0, a far more measured, controlled half than West Ham fans have been treated to in recent weeks.

From the old Bobby Moore Upper to the Billy Bonds' stand these days - I've been watching since '03 and a supporter since about 1970.. Favourite player - Dean Ashton: Curse you Shaun Wright-Phillips. I still watch YouTube repeats of the Cup Final of 2006 hoping in vain that Shaka Hislop grows another six inches and stops Steven Gerrard's injury time equaliser. Can tell I'm getting old knowing I watched both Mark Noble's debut and his last game at West Ham. Pulling on a Claret and Blue replica shirt still makes me feel the same butterflies as when I was seven years old. Magic.

False dawn as it so happens, not able to keep a clean sheet again!

On another day we’d win that game easily. Can’t fault the effort from the players. To hear some of our own fans booing and singing your not fit to wear the shirt is disgraceful. I thought those players gave everything they had and were extremely unlucky not to come away with something.

Glad Piroe playing, even though he is not ripping up any trees. Like others have said, good to have a no. 9 have a run of games and players around learn how he plays, where to find him.

Mayers under pressure and coping fine also with overlapping runs and creating some danger, great, but not many in the box each time. A bit of patience perhaps…

We will improve once we move on from the 5-a-side small man coaching.

We need rocks and cannons all over the pitch.

#2040. Is one point away from home ever a bad point? Fulham 1 Newcastle 1

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

In answer to the question above, the outcome at Craven Cottage definitely felt as if Newcastle United had dropped two rather than gained one, perhaps because we conceded a late equaliser.

Compared with May’s encounter, in what proved to be Eddie Howe’s final Premier League game as our head coach, the performance was much better, though still a long way below what I believe is possible.

Before kick-off I would have taken the draw. I said as much to a Fulham fan on the walk from Putney Bridge Tube station through Bishops Park. An American, she lives in Clapham and last season needed to choose a London club to support when her most recent serious relationship ended. No way would she continue to cheer for his team!

Her choice of Fulham was based partly on the club’s questionable claim to be the oldest in the capital. When I pointed out that in 147 years Fulham had never won a big trophy (domestic or European) she replied that she followed football for the fun, not the glory. An admirable attitude . . .

We shook hands and wished each other good luck at 2.30pm on the corner of the Riverside and Putney End stands. Another random conversation to add to the collection.

On the train up from Brighton I had quizzed an Arsenal fan, who was taking his two sons to The Emirates for the game against Hull.

What was his verdict on Bruno G? Why wasn’t our former captain a regular starter?

“We rotate nearly every match. Arteta picks him against teams who play a low block. I like Bruno because he’s always looking forward, trying to create. Lewis-Skelly is preferred in European games, which are more open. We also have Eze, who is probably 13th on the team sheet.”

A veritable wealth of riches for the title-winning manager.

Not that the Arsenal fan on the train had been confident last season, fearing the recent history of blowing their chances was likely to be repeated again.

Hadn’t Arsenal succeeded at last despite Arteta, rather than because of him, I suggested. The style of football was efficient rather than attractive. When we went to The Emirates in April, with Man City hot on Arsenal’s heels, the tension was palpable. An Eze cracker from a short corner routine saw them home that day. Another 1-0 to The Arsenal, just as they managed yesterday against Hull City.

How will they cope against Newcastle 2.0, when they meet at St James’ Park immediately after the international break? If United play to their full potential, with Sean Steur making things tick in midfield and Lewis Hall surging up the wing after quelling attacks, anything is possible. We proved that in the 2024/25 season, when we beat them three times.

Possible but unlikely, because we no longer have Isak and Gordon to fire the bullets supplied by Bruno G. Neither do we have the oh-so-predictable leadership of Howe; predictable as in getting the better of Arteta with pleasing frequency.

We lacked that sort of firepower yesterday. William Osula ran relentlessly to little effect. Yoane Wissa rarely showed the same enthusiasm. The chemistry between them looked embryonic, being charitable. The link play between Amar Dedic and Jacob Murphy on the right flank, between Hall and Harvey Barnes on the left, was sporadic to nonexistent.

When the full-backs advanced, the wide attackers dropped back. That was an understandable response to conceding three goals at Everton, four at Coventry and four at Leeds since mid-September. One consequence was a lot of sideways and backward passing, to the travelling fans’ frustration.

Another consequence was the need for Murphy and Barnes to defend if Fulham regained possession, which they did reasonably well.

With Steur and Nico Gonzalez in the middle of the park, supplemented by their wider teammates, United looked less open.

Matthias Jaissle has been widely blamed for trying to succeed with a two-man midfield. Yesterday the two was often a four, thanks to Dedic and Hall stepping up while Murphy and Barnes stepped back.

Total football it was not. It was, however, more encouraging than a lot of what we have seen in the German’s first three months in charge.

Dan Burn defended solidly and strode forward more than once, trying to make things happen. Malick Thiaw blocked and intercepted impressively from first to last, though his passing was occasionally alarming.

In the interests of research I watched the Everton v Coventry televised game on Friday evening. The referee at the Hill Dickinson was the biggest Homer since Ancient Greece, denying the visitors two penalties and ignoring a handball in Everton’s second goal. VAR refused to get involved just as Howard Webb, head of Pro Ref, wants.

I feared more of the same at Craven Cottage. Rob Jones didn’t disappoint. He was biased with a capital B, favouring the hosts whenever there was an element of doubt and often when there wasn’t. Fouls on visiting players went unpunished, whereas strong challenges by United were often penalised.

The first half contained only a few glimpses of fluid passing from either team. Lukas Hornicek made a couple of spectacular saves, while Barnes forced Bernd Leno to kick away a clever flick from a low Murphy cross. The Fulham keeper also stopped a goal-bound Barnes shot, this time unwittingly with his forehead.

Burn finished smartly at the near post from the resultant corner but the referee deemed Wissa had fouled Timothy Castagne with the sort of routine holding that is usually ignored by the officials.

After the interval United looked more dangerous as they attacked the Putney End that housed the vociferous Toon Army. Barnes cracked a right-foot curler off the outside of the post with Leno nowhere, Wissa was maybe two feet short of a tap-in from another low cross and for a few minutes Fulham struggled to break out of their half.

The replacement of Gonzalez and Wissa by Lewis Miley and Joe Willock on 61 minutes added to the threat. Steur was always available and kept the ball moving in midfield but struggled to recover from a heavy tackle. He made way for Matias Fernandez-Pardo, whose pace immediately unsettled Fulham.

When Murphy seized on a loose pass about 40 yards out on our right flank, he jinked inside, set his sights and with his left boot bent a sizzling shot beyond Leno. Mayhem among the travelling fans!

The cheers and chants were still bouncing around the stadium three minutes later when the equaliser went in. It has been credited to Rodrigo Muniz. Having watched the goal six times on television replays, I reckon Hall kicked the ball onto the Brazilian before it deflected off the diving Burn and into the net past a wrong-footed Hornicek. Perhaps a trip to Specsavers is needed . . .

Neither team were happy to settle for a point. A rapid break down the left led to Hall finding space 12 yards out. Sadly for him and his team, the ball was on his weaker boot and Leno was able to save the low shot.

Fulham could have stolen all three points in stoppage time when Ryan Sessegnon smashed a 20-yarder to Hornicek’s left. The young keeper dived across and parried it to safety, capping what was probably his best game so far for United.

One point gained or two dropped? I favour the latter verdict. We had the better chances in a tight game and should have taken three of them.

Newcastle are a work in progress. There’s plenty of room for improvement but there were enough signs yesterday to suggest we’re heading in the right direction.

Fulham 1 Newcastle United 1 – Saturday 7 November 2026 3pm

Shots on target were Newcastle 5 Fulham 5

Touches in the opposition box Newcastle 19 Fulham 27

Hornicek, Dedic, Thiaw (Schar 85), Burn, Hall, Gonzalez (Miley 61), Steur (Fernanez-Pardo 74), Barnes, Wissa (Willock 61), Murphy, Osula (Elanga 85)

#2039. Scotland's rivals reinstate under-fire duo after fake Covid certificate bans

Switzerland boss Murat Yakin insisted he never had any doubts about reinstating his captain Granit Xhaka and striker Breel Embolo to face Scotland in the Nations League.

Scotland face group leaders Switzerland in St Gallen during the latest international break, after a home game against North Macedonia.

The World Cup quarter-finalists have included veteran Sunderland star Xhaka and Atlanta United ace Embolo after they were both dumped from the previous four games in the competition following an investigation into them obtaining fake Covid certificates.

Xhaka and Embolo were handed suspended financial penalties, with Xhaka receiving a suspended fine of 150,000 Swiss francs and being placed on two years’ probation.

Ex-Celtic star tells Martin O'Neill why he's on receiving end of 'flak with love'

St Mirren sick of Old Firm 'hard luck' stories as Rangers come calling

Celtic revival or one-off resistance and is Duran the best player in Scotland?

And Yakin insisted he never hesitated in including them in his latest squad, where they face Slovenia too. He said: "That was never up for debate for me. Granit Xhaka is our leader.

"The only problem would have been if Manu Akanji, who stood in as captain in the last four games, had wanted to remain captain. But he sees Granit as the captain.

"We have a lot of battles for a place in the squad - the competition is very fierce. We have done well in this competition so far, and a point would be enough to win the group in our next match in Maribor.

"But we want to win every game in our group and maintain our 100 per cent record."

#2038. Blackburn Rovers 2 – 1 West Ham United | Final whistle, first impressions as new manager bounce falls flat

West Ham managed to overturn their recent sequence of dreadful, lethargic starts with bright first half performance against Blackburn Rovers. Both sides had their chances but West Ham’s attack dominated the first half, largely through Austbø and Ezra Mayers down the left hand side.

The Hammers set up with Engels the deepest midfielder sitting in front of the back four and Kanté plus Mukasa the more forward of the trio. It seemed to protect the back line a little better as, apart from one looped shot over Hermansen’s goal, Blackburn’s threat was contained during the first 45 minutes.

Three or four times in the first ’45 Mayers overlapped after combining with Austbø – looking far more potent a threat than Solomon who he’d replaced – and got excellent crosses in from the left, an attacking option that had been lacking with Morato as the full back.

Piroe headed against the post early in the second half after Austbo – again – twisted and turned on the left, and Engles crashed the rebound just wide. Waves of pressure developed on the Blackburn goal as the Hammers responded to their half time talk but against the run of play from a break down the other end, Blackburn took the lead through Gudjohnson who headed through Hermansen’s legs. West Ham behind again.

Parker responded with Solomon for Austbø who’d run his socks off for an hour and Taty appearing in place of Kanté.

Controversy as Rovers scored a second with Kilman prostrate after a head collision – Dapo Afolayan the ex West Ham boy fired one into the corner leaving West Ham with a mountain to climb. It must be said, naive defending from West Ham.

Joel Piroe grabbed one back after a lucky bounce sat nicely for him in the box: 2 – 1 with eight minutes to go and the Ewood Park atmosphere changed, the home fans nervy and the Hammers fans in full voice. The minutes ticked away and West Ham struggled to get the ball towards Blackburn’s box: Orford, a late substitute, very fortunate to avoid conceding a penalty in the closing minutes – once again the lack of VAR coming to West Ham’s rescue.

Five minutes of added time, West Ham looking as if they had neither the urgency or the ability to surge forward again, fiddling about on the edge of their own box with Hermansen being booed every time he touched the ball. One last chance as Soucek headed straight at the ‘keeper in the last few seconds and that was that. Poor. Very poor. So much possession and so little to show for it.

#2037. Fulham 1 Newcastle 1 match ratings and comments on all Newcastle United players

The independent voice of Newcastle United since 1988

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

Get your daily update and weekly newsletter by signing up today!

We asked Dave Marshall to give us his match ratings and comments on individual Newcastle United players after Fulham 1 Newcastle 1.

Nail-biting. Teeth gnashing. Unease. Anxiety. Growing disapproval. Such were the rumblings of a sizable, and growing, section of Newcastle supporters as United headed to west London for a date with Fulham.

The Cottagers a side going in just two points above relegation but showing signs of life in recent weeks.

A good omen for United going in, though: winning three on the bounce in the capital this season with no goals conceded.

But pressure mounting on Matthias Jaissle and the lads after a string of bad results.

While there are both positives and negatives to take from this performance and result v Fulham…

What’s most concerning is the vibe around the club.

It was noticeable Monday at St. James’ Park. And the ranting and raving online has reached ridiculous levels of theatre.

It was good that Newcastle had an away match after capitulating twice to the Merseyside Mackems because St. James’ Park would have been too toxic to have been any support for the black and white today.

This is not the place to debate Jaissle’s tenure or his seemingly increasingly tenuous position to remain United’s gaffer.

This is not the place to criticise the personnel decisions the brass have made in recent months.

Nor is to call out any players for lack of effort, skill, finishing, passing, common sense, etc.

But it is a place to remind you that we are Newcastle United.

And United supporters have a reputation for being among the most loyal, fervent, rabid, and supportive.

50,000 strong showed up on the regular even when having to endure seasons in the Championship.

Traveling Geordies are always lauded, especially on the continent. It’s no stretch to say that a lot of club brass around England are envious of the support Newcastle gets. Supporters who bleed black-and-white.

Think 50,000 would regularly show up if one of the Septics got relegated after so many years without any trophies and Mike Ashley the club owner?

(It’s still early, but we’re on course to find out next season… but I digress.)

Face it… this is nothing compared to the dark ages of the Fat Tub of Ashley years.

The struggles of a team that lost three of its top skill players and several of its top leaders and mostly replaced them with younger, greener, and arguably less-skilled footballers?

Not the worst times United supporters have ever endured.

The learning curve of a new gaffer who’s not been on the touchline even three months yet?

Not the worst depths Geordies have suffered through.

A string of bad performances, bad results, erratic play, defensive mishaps, poor finishing in front of the net…

Not happy with MJ’s tactics or his line-ups or his substitutions or his in-game management?

But what sucks more is the vibe of the supporters right now.

It’s as if a sizable portion of the fanbase is already certain that Matthias Jaissle is a failure and this team is not worthy of support.

The schedule ramps up in quality and intensity after this international break.

So it’s time for us as United supporters to ramp up our own intensity, passion, love, and support for the black-and-white.

Come matchday, it’s time to strap on our favourite United top and do nothing but get behind the team 100%.

When the season kicked off on August 23 at home to Liverpool, pretty much no one expected United to be on 12 points and hovering mid-table after Matchday 10.

Newcastle were tagged for relegation and left for Championship dead. So it’s fair to say that United have exceeded expectations so far.

It’s also easy to forget during a long season, particularly in the midst of a spell of bad results.

Anfield and Old Trafford get all the plaudits for being difficult venues for opponents.

But those of us who live and breathe English football know, even objectively, that no set of supporters gives its team that vital push more than the rabid throngs inside a pulsating St. James’ Park.

And that’s what we have to be again to get through this.

Lukas Hornicek – 8 Bounced back after the flub v Everton on Monday. Stood tall with five saves, several of them spectacular, including early on to deny Oscar Bobb and then a last-second stop to deny Sessegnon’s laserbolt in stoppage time. Can’t be faulted on the equaliser; nothing to be done once it deflected off BDB.

Amar Dedic – 6.5 While he seemed to handle Iwobi, he struggled with Robinson’s overlapping runs. Solid in the first half as United sat back, but lagged as the match went on, his 92nd-minute yellow card invited unnecessary pressure as the draw played out.

Malick Thiaw – 7 Much-needed athleticism was back on the backline. Composed, accurate for most of his time on the pitch. Didn’t clear the ball well enough in the build up to the equaliser.

Dan Burn – 6.5 Goal disallowed due to a soft foul by Wissa. Dominant in the air, and though unlucky for Muniz’s poke to deflect off him for the equaliser, not quick enough to close down the cross that led to it. Solid partnership with Thiaw.

Lewis Hall – 7 As good as we all think Hall to be, and no doubt we’re correct, to be truly world class, he’s got to bury that 88th-minute effort, even with his non-dominant right foot. Back to his usual level for the most part, otherwise.

Sean Steur – 6.5 Good to see him back and playing with confidence. Was tidy on the ball and always looking to direct passes forward. Still not sure about him being part of a two-man midfield. Not really sure about it generally speaking, to be fair.

Nico Gonzalez – 6 Had his moments in the middle of the park, but wonder about his fitness, as he was subbed for the 2nd game in a row on the hour mark. Though he helped United keep their shape, there was no creativity to his game to break down Fulham’s low block.

Yoane Wissa – 5 Will be aggrieved with the soft foul he got called for that cancelled Burn’s would-be goal. Still, can’t put himself in position for such a call. Had a couple of opportunities but made a meal of them. Didn’t trouble the GK as much as he should have.

Jacob Murphy – 8 A screaming curler that should’ve won it and was denied an assist for Burn’s header. A Murphinho performance that United needs more consistently from him, as he was Newcastle’s most consistent threat on the break.

Harvey Barnes – 6.5 Harsh? Maybe. But when you’re an “all-he-does-is-score” kind of footballer, you’ve got to put away at least one of the three glaring chances he didn’t. He caused Fulham all types of issues but not scoring is unforgivable and it cost United two points.

William Osula – 5 Was not the beneficiary of much good service but his inconsistent effort was disappointing, Did not get a shot on goal.

Lewis Miley – 6 Came on for Nico on 61’, vital defensive header to clear a dangerous Iwobi free-kick late but hope competition with Steur will have him passing more forward. Still, good to see him back.

Joe Willock – 6 On for Wissa on 61’, he added energy dynamism to the midfield but only managed 1 SOG, and it was from long range, not too troublesome.

Matias Fernandez-Pardo – 5 On for Steur on 74’, back for the first time in weeks. Late header was saved but not too much impact. Seemed to suffer a knock in stoppage time, so hope it’s not too serious.

Anthony Elanga – N/A (On too late to rate) On for Osula on 85’, no impact in this cameo.

Fabian Schar – N/A (On too late to rate) On for Thiaw on 85’ following the equaliser to help see things out.

Matthias Jaissle – 6 Not sure that this match set-up worked, not with our cast of characters. However, Jaissle’s plan to sit deep and counter was not a bad idea, given the past couple of weeks. A sniff of desperation? Not sure, but it almost worked perfectly. However, another failure to hold the lead. You can blame MJ all you want, but it was the same last season under Howe, and with a much different cast. It’s hard to explain. But it’s got to be fixed.

#2036. GdS: A combined salary less than Ramos’ – the story behind the Ferencvaros ‘miracle’

AC Milan’s opponents Ferencvaros are one of a few teams to have a perfect record in the Europa League, and their story is a fascinating one.

Ferencváros arrive at San Siro having won all three of their league phase games thus far. In addition to that, they are 20 unbeaten across all competitions and they will go top of their domestic league if they win their game in hand. La Gazzetta dello Sport (seen below) share some insight on the Hungarians.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Gonçalo Ramos’s gross salary €12.8m (€7m net including bonuses) is equivalent to the entire wage bill of Ferencváros. The combined salaries of the Hungarian club’s players total €11m.

Their highest earner is Naby Keïta, who accepted a contract worth just over €1.2m gross per season, seeking a career resurgence at the club with the largest payroll in the Hungarian league.

The Serbian midfielder Birmančević – formerly of Sparta Prague and Getafe, who arrived last summer – earns a slightly lower salary. Meanwhile, attacking midfielder Zachariassen earns around €700k and has scored three goals so far, as has Alphadjo Cissé.

In terms of wages, therefore, there is simply no comparison between the Rossoneri and Ferencváros. Yet, the Hungarians have won every match, while Milan have only three points. All the more reason not to take them lightly.

Gabor Kubatov has been on the board of Ferencváros since 2010, becoming president a year later. Under his leadership, the club has won eight Hungarian league titles. His personal history is quite unique: as a young man, he was a regular in ‘Sector 2’ – the section occupied by the ultras.

He later changed paths, and in 2006, he became a member of parliament, representing Fidesz, the party of Viktor Orbán. Despite his own background in the stands, his relationship with the Ferencváros ultras has not always been smooth.

In 2014, in an effort to combat violence and incidents of racism, Kubatov introduced a biometric identification system for stadium entry. A segment of the most ardent supporters responded by boycotting home matches, a protest that lasted for over three years.

An agreement was finally reached and the fans returned to the stands. With their support, Ferencváros went on to win seven consecutive league titles.

On 10 December 2017, a young Adam Nagy faced Milan while playing for Bologna. It didn’t go well: a 2-1 victory for the Rossoneri. Today, Nagy returns as a far more mature leader of his ‘miracle’ Ferencváros side.

Indeed, a significant portion of the Hungarian midfielder’s career has unfolded in Italy. He spent three years with the Rossoblù from 2016 to 2019 – following his initial breakthrough at Ferencváros – before returning to Italy in 2021 to join Pisa, having previously left to try his hand at Bristol City in England.

His most recent stint was with Spezia, which he departed this summer to return to his homeland. Yesterday, in a press conference, Rúben Amorim spoke very highly of him: “He is very skilled in the initial phase of build-up play.”

His ability to circulate the ball deep in his own half is his greatest strength. Conversely, he rarely ventures into the final third. The proof? Throughout all his years in Italy, he scored only one goal: against Verona in Serie A.

From the European champions Liverpool to Ferencvaros. Naby Keita – who will start on the bench tonight, hasn’t had the career he hoped for. Liverpool paid €65m to sign him from RB Leipzig in 2018, he won six more trophies in addition to the Champions League with Klopp’s English side.

In 2023, the Guinean midfielder moved to Werder Bremen, where he was left out of the squad after refusing to travel for the trip to Leverkusen because he wouldn’t have been a starter. Since January 2025, he has been at Ferencváros, who acquired him a year later.

Wearing a Liverpool shirt, Keïta has already beaten Milan at San Siro on 7 December 2021, a defeat that contributed to the Diavolo being eliminated in the group stage.

A less pleasant memory for Keïta involves his encounter with Luka Modrić when he came on in the final minutes of the 2022 Champions League final, which Liverpool lost to Real Madrid.

#2035. Player Ratings: Blackburn 2-1 West Ham as Hermansen Has a Nightmare

West Ham’s promising start at Ewood Park ultimately counted for very little as Scott Parker’s side slipped to a 2-1 defeat against Blackburn Rovers. Despite enjoying plenty of possession and creating opportunities, the Hammers were undone by poor defending and some particularly questionable goalkeeping.

Joël Piroe’s late goal gave West Ham a chance of rescuing something, but the longer the game went on, the worse we seemed to play. There were some decent individual performances, particularly early on, but others will want to forget this afternoon in a hurry.

A really poor afternoon for the goalkeeper. I thought he could have been far more commanding for Blackburn’s opening goal, whether that meant catching the cross, punching it or simply getting something on the ball. He did make a straightforward late save from Todd Cantwell, but that doesn’t change my overall assessment.

One of West Ham’s more reliable performers before being substituted. Made some useful defensive interceptions and regularly pushed forward to support Bowen down the right. Tried a couple of long throws into the penalty area, although they didn’t really cause Blackburn much trouble.

Had some positive moments going forward, including a driving run from defence and a header that went narrowly wide early in the second half. However, I thought he could have done better for Blackburn’s first goal, and his performance deteriorated badly towards the end. Was fortunate not to concede a penalty before slipping twice during a dreadful passage of play that handed Blackburn a dangerous counter-attack.

Probably West Ham’s most dependable defender on the day. Made several important interceptions, particularly down the left where Blackburn repeatedly threatened, and was willing to carry the ball forward to help build attacks. Also produced a decent cross for Castellanos, although the resulting header went wide.

A mixed afternoon for the youngster. I was impressed with his willingness to get forward, his passing combinations with Austbø and some of the crosses he delivered. However, Blackburn repeatedly targeted his side, often leaving him facing two opponents, and he was beaten too easily in the build-up to the opening goal. Still very much learning the position.

Didn’t think he had a particularly good game. Had plenty of involvement, took the corners and got himself into shooting positions, but too often the final product was disappointing. Lost possession unnecessarily on occasions, failed to close down Blackburn’s second goalscorer quickly enough and wasted a promising late free kick with poor delivery.

You certainly couldn’t fault his work rate. At times he seemed to be everywhere, covering at left-back, appearing on the right and getting forward to support the attack. However, he wasn’t nearly as influential on the ball as he had been during the second half against Cardiff, and his shooting was disappointing. Replaced by Castellanos after 64 minutes.

One of West Ham’s more inventive players, particularly during the first half. Looked to move the ball quickly, attempted some clever through passes and wasn’t afraid to shoot, forcing one save and seeing another effort deflected behind. Not everything worked, but at least he was trying to make things happen.

I was genuinely surprised when he was substituted because he’d been one of West Ham’s livelier attacking players. Produced a lovely dribble past two defenders in the first half, linked up well with Mayers and delivered an excellent cross that Bowen headed against the post. Could perhaps have offered Mayers more defensive protection before Blackburn’s opener, but I thought he was contributing plenty going forward.

Blackburn 2-1 West Ham: Austbo was one of the Hammers better players

Worked hard to make things happen and was heavily involved in West Ham’s attacking play, particularly from the right. Unlucky to see his header strike the post following Austbø’s cross, while a difficult chance from close range went wide as he was falling and sliding. Also produced a lovely chipped delivery for Souček’s late header, but couldn’t quite provide the decisive contribution West Ham needed.

A frustrating performance rescued to some extent by an excellent goal. Too often he seemed hesitant in promising positions, allowing defenders to recover, while one particularly poor pass in the second half wasted a good attacking opportunity. However, he reacted brilliantly to Castellanos’ cross in the 82nd minute, firing high into the roof of the net. Whatever else you say about his performance, he took that chance extremely well.

Replaced Austbø after 58 minutes and was practically anonymous. Considering how involved Austbø had been, the substitution certainly didn’t improve West Ham’s attacking threat down the left.

Introduced for Kanté after 64 minutes and provided the cross that led to Piroe’s goal. Also had a header go wide from a Kilman delivery and was involved in the scramble that presented Bowen with a difficult chance. At least contributed something tangible to the attack.

Didn’t have a great deal of time to influence proceedings, particularly with West Ham having already lost their shape. Played one very silly ball into Orford inside our own penalty area, creating unnecessary danger. However, he also got into one of those familiar goalscoring positions in stoppage time, only to direct his header straight at the goalkeeper from Bowen’s excellent delivery.

Another substitute who came into a team that had lost its shape and was struggling for confidence. Was put in a difficult position by Souček’s poor pass inside the penalty area and was fortunate not to concede a penalty. Difficult to judge him too harshly given the limited time he had on the pitch and the state of the game when he entered.

It has been tough for many Newcastle United players this season.

Newcastle United players that are new to the club and in so many cases, new to the country and the Premier League.

Throw in the fact United have experienced more injuries this season than any other Premier League club and it adds another level.

It has been a tough watch at times for us as fans but I think as the season goes on, we can see a much better team and season develop.

There has been no continuity, largely down to the injuries, plus of course a manager still finding his feet after arriving only 18 days before the season started and a squad of Newcastle United players that didn’t get a proper run together in pre-season.

My belief is that as the season develops these six Newcastle United players can take NUFC forward, in the forward positions…of midfield and attack:

20 Lewis Miley 18 Sean Steur 24 Nico Gonzalez 20 Bazoumana Toure 21 Matias Fernandez-Pardo 23 William Osula

An average of only 21 for this half dozen and Matthias Jaissle has been trying his best to protect the likes of Steur, Toure and MFP.

Osula and Miley have missed so many matches through injury this season and Lewis Miley ending up playing right-back when he has played usually!

Nico Gonzalez is still bedding in and used to playing every match, rarely with the same teammates in midfield!

With time I think MFP and Toure can be big assets.

I will revisit this later in the season as to how this six have got on…

#2033. Blackburn Rovers 2- 1 West Ham | Boos and ironic cheers highlight massive concern

THERE was an ironic cheer from the West Ham away supporters at about 88 minutes, which considering their team was 2- 1 down and looking clueless was even more remarkable.

The cheer was for Mads Hermansen finally making a save, with a shot hit straight at him being pretty much the first time he’d connected with anything, as another two goals had found their way under and past the hapless Dane.

7000 West Ham fans had made the trip to Blackburn in expectation of a triumphant start to Parker’s era and yet saw their starting eleven dominate the ball but fail to score. Hermansen had dealt with a smattering of booing from his own fans ever since Rovers took the lead with a header that went between the Dane’s legs.

Times’ up, Mads. The big concern was that Scott Parker picked him ahead of Areola. We told him….

Hardly a confidence boost for the young keeper who surely should not have been selected in the first place.

No criticism through could be attached to Hermansen for Blackburn’s second goal but West Ham found themselves two goals behind, chasing the game and seemingly nothing to offer, back passing and fiddling around in the last few minutes.

Parker can have no excuse now for continuing to select his hapless keeper. The Dane plays as if he’s got arthritic knees (take it fromm one who knows) and doesn’t dive for anything, just collapsing to the left or right, week after week.

Whatever issue there may be with second-in-line Alphonse Areola, he simply has to start after the international break.

Otherwise, we may as well simply drape a goal keeper’s jersey on the cross bar: It’ll be about as effective.

The most frustrating thing? We called this, as did just about every West Ham fan: Hermansen is just not good enough.

#2032. Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall: Thomas Tuchel makes feelings clear on Everton star after England omission

By Oliver Thomas | 06 Nov 2026 14:10, Last updated: 06 Nov 2026 14:11

Thomas Tuchel has admitted that Everton midfielder Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall was “very close” to earning a maiden England call-up for November’s international break.

The 28-year-old has established himself as an important first-team player for the Toffees since joining in August 2025, recording 10 goals and eight assists in 44 appearances.

Dewsbury-Hall is one of the first names on the Everton teamsheet under manager David Moyes, starting all nine Premier League matches in an advanced midfield position this season and chipping in with two goals.

The former Leicester City and Chelsea man delivered two standout performances for the Toffees in back-to-back wins over Newcastle United in the EFL Cup and Premier League, enhancing his case for recognition at senior international level.

Moyes is a huge admirer of Dewsbury-Hall and recently stated that the midfielder is “knocking on the door” for an England call-up.

"Thank goodness I don't have to pick the England team because they have so many good players to choose from,” Moyes told reporters on Thursday.

"Kiernan's form is getting back to his levels of last year. I hope he does [get the call-up]. He'll certainly be knocking on the door."

Tuchel has since confirmed that Dewsbury-Hall is among a group of 55 players who are in contention for England selection, but he has narrowly missed out on this occasion.

Speaking about Dewsbury-Hall at press conference on Friday, Tuchel said: "Very good player, very good season. A very good football player overall.

"In the way we play now, I don't see him in the central midfield in the build-up, but in the finishing part as an offensive No.8 or almost as a No.10.

"He's in our 55 and a standout player for Everton. We see his quality and he's a nice watch because he's a very good football player. He was very close.”

Tuchel has opted to call up Borussia Dortmund’s Jobe Bellingham and Fulham’s Joshua King for the first time, while Everton’s James Garner, Jude Bellingham, Elliot Anderson, Declan Rice and Myles Lewis-Skelly are five more midfielders selected.

Dewsbury-Hall is not the only notable midfield omission from Tuchel’s latest squad, with Cole Palmer, Kobbie Mainoo and Phil Foden also left out, while Alex Scott is absent due to injury.

From a selfish perspective, many Everton fans would prefer to see Dewsbury-Hall rest up and not sustain an injury during international duty, but many others believe that the midfielder now deserves his chance to represent the Three Lions.

Dewsbury-Hall is expected to start for Everton in tonight’s Premier League clash at home against Frank Lampard’s Coventry City.

Everton duo Garner and Jarrad Branthwaite are also expected to feature against Coventry before linking up with the England squad, with Tuchel previously highlighting the qualities of both players.

"I am very happy, [Garner is] our mini [Federico] Valverde. He's getting there and he played very, very good,” Tuchel said in March.

"I was quite sure that he would play well because he has this natural confidence and he's very physical; he won a lot of balls.

“There are some situations where he can be a bit more open and drive through midfield with the ball with a little bit more confidence… But I am very impressed with the way he trained, and the way he behaves.”

On Branthwaite, Tuchel said in September: “We’ve had Jarrad on our radar for a long time. We see big potential in him... He’s fast, tall and has a strong left foot. It’s good to see him over a long period and give him a chance.”

England will face Croatia and Spain in their final two UEFA Nations League fixtures, playing host to the former at Wembley on November 12 and travelling to Madrid to take on the latter three days later.

#2031. West Ham Go Full Circle as Blackburn Expose Familiar Problems

West Ham’s 2-1 defeat against Blackburn Rovers was a particularly frustrating result because, for large periods of the game, Scott Parker’s side appeared to be the better team. We started brightly, enjoyed plenty of possession and created opportunities, yet somehow managed to leave Ewood Park with nothing.

What concerns me most isn’t necessarily the result itself, although that’s bad enough. It’s the manner in which West Ham gradually deteriorated as the afternoon progressed. Even after Joël Piroe pulled a goal back late on, I thought we looked increasingly disorganised and short of confidence.

And that’s perhaps the strangest aspect of Parker’s first two matches. We started against Cardiff looking completely devoid of confidence, rediscovered it during that extraordinary second-half comeback, began confidently against Blackburn and somehow finished looking just as nervous as we had before.

I was actually quite encouraged by the opening stages. West Ham pressed high, moved the ball around reasonably well and looked determined to take the game to Blackburn. Max Kilman was particularly proactive, stepping out of defence to offer an additional passing option, while Divine Mukasa and Arne Engels were regularly involved in midfield.

Down the left, Ezra Mayers and Edvin Austbø developed a promising partnership. Mayers was willing to get forward and Austbø looked lively, producing one lovely piece of skill to beat two Blackburn players before delivering a dangerous cross.

Blackburn 2-1 West Ham: Austbo was one of the Hammers better players

However, there was a problem developing on that side of the pitch. Blackburn repeatedly managed to isolate Mayers against two opponents, and while the youngster was doing some good things offensively, he wasn’t receiving enough protection defensively.

Joël Piroe was also struggling to make the most of promising situations. On one occasion, he found himself with only a single defender to beat but hesitated for so long that three opponents eventually surrounded him. West Ham were having plenty of the ball, but Blackburn were defending deeply and making it difficult to create clear opportunities.

The second half initially offered more encouragement. Mavropanos headed narrowly wide from an Engels corner, Piroe had an effort saved and then Austbø produced an excellent cross which Bowen headed against the post. At that stage, West Ham were piling on the pressure and Blackburn were struggling to get out of their own half.

Then came the sucker punch. In the 54th minute, Blackburn broke down their right, with Mayers unable to stop the delivery into the penalty area. Andri Guðjohnsen converted, but I thought several West Ham players could have done better.

Austbø might have provided more protection for Mayers, Mavropanos could have defended the situation better and I certainly felt Mads Hermansen should have been more commanding. Whether he caught the cross, punched it or simply got something on the ball, I thought the goalkeeper had an opportunity to intervene.

It was a horrible goal to concede, particularly given how much of the attacking West Ham had been doing. Parker responded by introducing Manor Solomon for Austbø, a substitution I found surprising. The Norwegian had been one of our more involved attacking players, while Solomon subsequently struggled to make any impression.

Mohamadou Kanté was then replaced by Taty Castellanos, but West Ham were finding it increasingly difficult to establish the same attacking rhythm. Blackburn’s second goal arrived in the 71st minute, with Afolayan producing an excellent finish.

Kilman had gone down following contact to his face, but too many West Ham players appeared more interested in appealing for a foul than dealing with the danger. Engels, in particular, could have done more to close down the shot. Whatever the circumstances, you cannot simply stop defending because you believe the referee should have awarded a free kick.

At 2-0, the game appeared to be slipping away, but West Ham eventually found a route back through something remarkably straightforward. Castellanos got down the right-hand side and delivered a dangerous ball into the penalty area. Piroe reacted quickly and fired high into the roof of the net in the 82nd minute.

It was an excellent finish from a striker who, in truth, hadn’t been having a particularly good afternoon. But sometimes football really is that simple. Get the ball wide, get down the line and deliver something dangerous into the box. Give your centre-forward an opportunity to attack the ball.

Suddenly it was Blackburn 2-1 West Ham, with enough time remaining to rescue a point. Unfortunately, the expected late onslaught never really materialised. In fact, I thought West Ham became progressively worse.

Mavropanos endured a dreadful few minutes, fortunate not to concede a penalty before slipping and gifting Blackburn a counter-attack. He then slipped again while attempting to recover, while Souček subsequently played a very poor pass into Lewis Orford inside our own penalty area, creating another potentially disastrous situation.

West Ham looked increasingly nervous, and the defensive organisation seemed to disappear. There were still opportunities at both ends in stoppage time, with Todd Cantwell shooting straight at Hermansen when Blackburn might have made it 3-1.

Souček then headed directly at the Blackburn goalkeeper following an excellent chipped delivery from Bowen. It was precisely the sort of position from which we’ve seen Souček score numerous times, but once again West Ham had failed to make the most of a promising opportunity.

I keep coming back to the confidence issue because I think it explains an awful lot about what we’ve witnessed over these two matches. Against Cardiff, West Ham were absolutely dreadful during the opening 45 minutes, before producing a transformation after half-time that was almost impossible to believe.

Suddenly the players looked confident, aggressive and capable of playing some very good football. That improvement appeared to carry into the opening stages at Ewood Park, where we pressed Blackburn, moved the ball with purpose and looked considerably more comfortable in possession.

Yet by the closing stages, the confidence had completely evaporated. It was almost as though we’d gone full circle in the space of two matches, ending up precisely where we started. That is particularly disappointing because I still believe this West Ham squad possesses considerably more ability than recent performances suggest.

There were some positives. Mukasa showed invention, Austbø looked dangerous, Kilman had a decent game and Piroe took his goal extremely well. But the defensive mistakes, poor decision-making and increasingly nervous football were all too familiar.

I don’t think Scott Parker can be held responsible for everything we’ve witnessed this week. He’s barely had any meaningful time on the training pitch, and the international break offers him an opportunity to start properly implementing his ideas.

However, the evidence of these two games suggests that restoring confidence isn’t simply a matter of delivering one rousing team talk. The psychological side of West Ham’s problems may be every bit as important as the tactical side.

The frustrating thing is that we’ve already seen how much better these players can perform when they believe in themselves. Against Blackburn, we watched that belief gradually disappear again.

Kris Gonzo (commonly known to the West Ham community as Gonzo) is the co-founder of Hammers Chat (established 2014) and the lead video content creator and columnist for Claret and Hugh.

With over a decade of professional sports media experience, he is a frequent West Ham United analyst and contributor for Sky Sports News, BBC Football Focus, and BBC Radio 5 Live. He previously served as an official video and content creator for West Ham United FC during the club's tenure at Upton Park and featured in the official documentary commemorating the historic final game at the Boleyn Ground.

A lifelong Hammer since the legendary 10-0 victory over Bury, when he isn't providing daily match analysis on the Hammers Chat YouTube Channel or broadcasting on X (@GONZObignose), he can be found walking his dog and restoring classic pinball machines.

Scott Parker’s words at full time pretty much summed up the remainder of this Championship season for West Ham United following the side’s first away defeat of the campaign. The new manager bounce failed to materialise as his squad thew away chance after chance against their solid opponents who twice capitalised on the now-traditional lacklustre Irons’ defending.

Speaking after the game to BBC Radio London, a hoarse Hammers head coach declared :

Not only at Ewood Park, but in the 31 remaining games of this season. A six point gap between the Hammers in ninth and the league leaders is not yet insurmountable. But it is, certainly, a mountain to climb for Parker to turn West Ham’s dreadfully mediocre-looking squad into Championship contenders.

With so many leaks, it is difficult to know which hole to plug first in the slowly sinking good ship West Ham United. Goalkeeper, defence, midfield, attack – all are areas crying out for urgent post-Nuno repair.. But none are yet beyond salvage.

A tough watch – Scott Parker will have learned a lot about his West Ham squad

As many have commented, though, it’s going to be a long season.

Right now, half a season of the dour, drab, boring but solid wins for which Scott Parker received so much criticism from his time at Burnley would be pretty well received in east London.

Usually we curse the international break but I have a feeling this time around it comes as a huge relief to the manager, the squad and supporters, for very different reasons. Amongst supporters, optimism will no doubt resurface at some stage during the next fortnight as we convince ourselves that if nothing else, we have the right man for the job at the helm.

Whatever Scott Parker is getting paid, if he somehow manages to transform this group into his trademark mean, lean, tough side capable of grinding out one-nil victories week in, week out, frankly he’ll be worth every penny.

#2028. “Erased” – Media explanation for one star’s waning at West Ham United

West Ham’s Nuno- divided squad was rallied midweek by new manager Scott Parker with his declaration that the slate had been wiped clean and that everyone had a chance to impress. Indeed as if to prove the point his first match day squad included Soungoutou Magassa, one of the summer want-aways who didn’t get his way.

Rather than accepting that the West Ham management simply don’t rate their skipper, the understandably patriotic local media indulge themselves in all manner of excuses for their star’s waning in east London.

Edson Alvarez pictured back in training in Parker’s pre-Blackburn session.

“91 days in oblivion, with Alvarez still erased from West Ham.

Hispanic Post went further, arguing in an opinion piece that the exclusion points to a deep fracture between the player and the London club’s project.”

Whereas the first two sides picked may well have been a ‘committee’ selection involving his coaching team, since the new manager only rocked up on Wednesday, two weeks with virtually his whole squad including the likes of Magassa and Alvarez will allow Parker to judge for himself who has the cojones to give his West Ham line up some much-needed moral fibre.

Should Alvarez still not feature, then the Mexican media will simply have to drop the conspiracy theories and face the fact that successive West Ham managers just don’t think he’s good enough for second tier English football.

Before joining Middlesbrough, Cozier-Duberry enjoyed an outstanding loan spell with Bolton Wanderers in League One last season. He scored 11 goals and contributed 13 assists, underlining his reputation as one of the country’s most promising young attacking talents.

It will be fascinating to see how Cozier-Duberry’s loan campaign at Middlesbrough develops over the course of the season. However, any suggestion that he was close to wearing a claret-and-blue shirt appears to be wide of the mark.

#2026. West Ham fans’ furious reaction raises an uncomfortable question

As the Hammers subsided to their first away defeat in the Championship, long suffering supporters, who’d undertaken the 480 mile round trip to be served up a pretty spineless team performance, decided to let their team have it with both barrels.

After last week’s displeasure culminating an Hammers fans singing ‘sacked in the morning’ to their own manager, this weekend brought the players into the crosshairs as the next logical target for their ire.

..With Nuno Espirito Santo out of the job and with Scott Parker just 72 hours in, the 7,500+ travelling fans turned on their stars.

Under no illusions after the result – and the away fans’ response – yesterday: Scott Parker

..As well as booing their own goal keeper pretty much throughout, if the reports on the radio were correct.

Traditionalists will likely be aghast at the thought of fans undermining their own team in this manner, whilst those who participated no doubt feel it was the only way to show their contempt for the perceived lack of commitment and effort which those eleven representatives  of the Claret and Blue heritage displayed.

Not to mention the hundreds of pounds it costs each supporter, every game, merely to arrive at the turnstiles in support of our club. But is it the ‘right’ thing to do?

For me – it’s a no. I started attending games with my son when he was ten years old and however bad it got (it was pretty dire in that season of 2003-4) we never left early, never booed our own players (Luis Boa Morte excepted, I must confess to once letting my frustration with his indolence bubble over) and always, always applauded those who’d put in a shift, regardless of outcome. And I’d not even heard ‘you’re not fit to wear the shirt‘ sung by West Ham fans in my couple of decades’ worth of attending games.

I just don’t see it helping team morale or positively influencing the final outcome. Which is, after all, the point of ‘supporters’.

Giving ‘The Sun’ another gleeful headline to point out our sufferings sticks in my throat too.

But don’t get me wrong, each has absolutely the right to their own response. Just don’t see it helping is all.

Bryan Mbeumo and Matheus Cunha have both played through the middle this season, but it is understood that the 20-time English champions want to bring in a new centre-forward during the January transfer window.

Leeds United's Dominic Calvert-Lewin and Al-Ahli's Ivan Toney have both recently been linked with moves to Old Trafford.

Meanwhile, it is understood that Jean-Philippe Mateta is also an option given that his contract with Crystal Palace will expire at the end of the campaign.

According to The Sun, Fulham's Muniz has now emerged as a potential option.

The report claims that Muniz's lack of football this season could see him leave in January, and Man United are considering him as a short-term fix.

The 25-year-old played under Michael Carrick at Middlesbrough during a loan spell in 2022-23, so he is known to the Man United head coach.

Muniz has scored twice in 10 appearances for Fulham this season, but he has failed to find the back of the net in seven outings in the Premier League.

The Brazilian has a record of 29 goals and four assists in 132 matches for Fulham in all competitions, including 18 goals and three assists in 85 Premier League games.

Muniz's best season at Fulham came in 2024-25, when he netted 11 times in 36 appearances in all competitions, but he only struck once in 25 matches for his London club last term.

It remains to be seen whether Carrick stays in charge of Man United heading into the January transfer window, but the Red Devils must add a forward to their squad in the winter.

#2024. GdS: Milan’s €500m Adidas deal causes reaction from rivals Inter – the situation

Inter are looking enviously at their city rivals AC Milan once again after Saturday’s derby, with the news of the record Adidas deal emerging.

As reported by La Gazzetta dello Sport on Wednesday, under the new agreement Adidas will pay Milan €50m per year for ten seasons starting from 2028-29. This is when the collaboration with PUMA ends, who currently pay €24.5m per year, as per the last accounts.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

The paper (via Calciomercato.com) go on to state that it is likely that the €50m yearly figure includes sporting bonuses, such as participation in the Champions League, the value of material supplies (value in kind) and a portion to be invested in promotional activities (marketing fund).

Contracts with kit makers are not limited to recognising the value of just the home, away, third and other shirts, but can extend to the sale of related products. Then, guaranteed minimums and royalties come into play that are triggered above a certain turnover threshold.

For example, in addition to the €24.5m from PUMA, €55.8m in revenues came from store, e-commerce and merchandising/licensing activities, in particular those relating to the contract with the same German company and those from licensing with Fanatics and MatchWornShirt.

As for Inter, the renewal with Nike – effective from 2023 – resulted in a 70% increase over the previous contract, but the €28m per year is not in line with the club’s current commercial value. In addition to the Milan-Adidas deal, Juventus currently get €46m per year from Adidas (€41m from 2027-28).

Inter have maintained their merchandising revenues internally, over €35m in 2025-26 thanks to the new business model introduced with Fanatics, but Nike’s €28m is too little according to the Nerazzurri’s commercial management.

The contract expires in 2031, and La Gazzetta report that they will seek to renegotiate the deal to avoid accumulating delays over the next five years. Considering that Juventus and Milan have committed to the next decade, Inter have leverage as the only one of the ‘big three’ up for grabs.

#2023. Falkirk warned over Hearts injury crisis ahead of Tynecastle test

Falkirk manager John McGlynn has told his players to ignore talk of a Hearts injury crisis as they prepare for Sunday’s visit to Tynecastle.

Hearts head coach Wouter Vrancken’s selection problems mounted further on Thursday when Stephen Kingsley picked up a hamstring injury in his team’s Europa League defeat by Thun in Switzerland.

Days earlier Hearts had lost Thomas Magnusson to concussion and former Falkirk midfielder Calvin Miller to a knee injury that will keep him out for two months.

Vrancken is now missing a full team of players with Harry Milne, Christian Borchgrevink, Oisin McEntee, Ageu, Craig Halkett, Blair Spittal, Tom Renaud and Oisin McEntee all out.

But McGlynn is wary of the strength in depth of his former club.

“They’ve not been beaten at home (in the league) in 18-19 months,” said McGlynn, who recently lost full-backs Leon McCann and Ryan Strain to thigh injuries.

“They’ve got a proud record there and it’s not going to be easy. Yeah, they’ve got injuries, absolutely, it’s a fact. But they can still put 11 good players on the park. They might be a little bit lighter on the bench, but they can still put a good 11 players on the pitch.

“We’re not going to get too caught up in the injuries that they have. I sympathise with the manager, he’s restricted in the players he’s got to choose from. I sympathise with the players who are getting injured.

“But we’ve got to focus on our job and not get too caught up in that.

“You end up coming a cropper if you’re thinking that they’ve got all these players injured, and it’s just a matter of turning up.

“We know that’s not going to be the case and that’s the message that I’m giving to our players.”

Vrancken told Hearts TV: “The situation we’re in, we have to just stick together and fight again on Sunday.

“It’s an important run of games like we already know, and make sure that we are as fit as possible to go for the game.

“It is good that it’s a Tynecastle, so we have a full stadium behind us and that has to give the energy to make it this last game before the break a good one.”

#2022. Wimborne Town vs Crawley Town - prediction, team news, lineups

By Carter White | 06 Nov 2026 14:23, Last updated: 06 Nov 2026 14:45

Aiming to cause an almighty upset in the first round of this season's FA Cup, Wimborne Town welcome League Two outfit Crawley Town to Wyatt Homes Stadium on Sunday afternoon.

The Magpies have navigated a couple of qualification hurdles to reach this famous stage of the competition, whereas the Red Devils have spent recent times struggling in the fourth tier.

Competing in the Southern League Premier Division, Wimborne Town are currently sat in the seventh tier of the English football pyramid, meaning that it is a great achievement to even reach the FA Cup first round.

The Magpies have battled through four rounds of qualifying to book a tie with League Two side Crawley this weekend, beating Portishead Town, Weston-Super-Mare, Moneyfields and Chelmsford City.

Wimborne come into this winner-takes-all clash in good form, unbeaten in five matches (W4 D1) across all competitions, enjoying a 2-0 home success over Chippenham Town last weekend.

Bagging a brace in the Wyatt Homes success last time out, Joe Smith leads the Magpies' Golden Boot race with five seventh-tier strikes, also scoring in the 3-0 home triumph over Gosport Borough on October 20.

Bidding to reach the National League South, Wimborne are currently occupying ninth spot in the Southern Premier Division standings, just three points behind Chichester City in the lowest of the playoff spots.

Crawley Town will be looking for back-to-back wins for the first time since early April this weekend after winning 1-0 at Oldham Athletic on Halloween, ending a nine-game winless run (D3 L6) in the fourth tier.

The Red Devils were helped massively by their hosts receiving two red cards within the opening 30 minutes at Boundary Park, where a Danilo Orsi strike proved enough to defeat nine men.

Despite picking up their maiden league success since August last weekend, Crawley are still rooted to the very bottom of the League Two standings, three points behind the safety of Rotherham United in 22nd spot.

For all of their league struggles, the Red Devils enjoyed a marvellous result in their most recent cup match, putting four goals past League One Bromley without reply in the EFL Trophy on October 6.

Although Crawley will wear their favourites tags with pride this weekend, they are also fully aware that shock results can occur, with Scott Lindsey's Red Devils losing in the first round of the FA Cup at National League Boreham Wood last season.

Netting the winning goal in the tie with Chelmsford, Antonio Diaz will be looking to impress for Wimborne against EFL opposition this weekend.

Max Bustamante is also a dangerous attacking option for the Magpies, who will need to take advantage of their rare offensive moments on Saturday.

Bringing experience to a potential slip-up situation, Vito Mannone should start in goal for Crawley at Wyatt Homes.

After keeping a clean sheet at Oldham last time out, Jonny Russell and Priestley Farquharson should remain as the centre-back pairing.

Looking to captain the side through a difficult away trip, Jude Arthurs is set to start in the heart of midfield.

Plain; Walker, Roberts, Wright; Sullivan, Yang, Wooding, Roundell, Munn; Smith, Diaz

Mannone; Gordon, Farquharson, Russell, Richards; Barker, Arthurs; Duke-McKenna, Aderoju, Morgan; Orsi

Currently on a winning run at Wyatt Homes Stadium, Wimborne will be confident of producing a respectable display this weekend.

However, Crawley possess the EFL quality and should have enough power to book a spot in the second round.

#2021. Sunderland vs Chelsea - prediction, team news, lineups

By Ben Knapton | 06 Nov 2026 14:33, Last updated: 06 Nov 2026 17:48

Needing nothing short of a minor miracle to replicate their 2025-26 feats against Chelsea, Sunderland host the Blues in Sunday's Premier League fixture at the Stadium of Light.

The Black Cats trail their visitors by 16 places and 11 points in the Premier League table at the time of writing and face Xabi Alonso's well-rested men after a sobering defeat in Europe too.

The meeting between two erstwhile Premier League midfield maestros last weekend saw Alonso pile more misery onto Michael Carrick, whose Manchester United side had the better of the opening 45 minutes at Stamford Bridge before an all-too familiar implosion.

Morgan Rogers waltzed his way past a disorganised Red Devils defence to propel the Blues into the lead, before Lisandro Martinez's senseless red card and Cole Palmer's penalty put paid to any hopes of a Mancunian fightback.

Snapping a two-game losing sequence in all competitions and earning their third win from their last four Premier League matches, Chelsea's triumph coupled with Liverpool losing to Arsenal saw the Blues consolidate fourth spot in the rankings, one clear of the Reds and three worse off than Brighton & Hove Albion.

The Blues' sorry defeat to Tottenham Hotspur raised questions about how Alonso's squad can cope in the absence of influential attacker Joao Pedro, but Chelsea answered those critics in gameweek nine to earn their first Premier League home win with a clean sheet since January.

Fifteen goals conceded still makes the visitors the worst defensive unit in the top 10, though, while they have shipped eight in five away games in all tournaments; seven of those came in their first three road matches, though, and they have since allowed just one in their last two on rival turf.

However, Alonso's side now square up to one of the four teams with a worse backline tally than them in the 2026-27 Premier League, and one without Chelsea's colossal firepower to make up for it.

The second season syndrome cliche is very much appropriate for Sunderland, whose measly five-point total places them bottom of the Premier League standings, although 17th-placed Man United are only two points better off.

The Black Cats have shown little signs of survival spirit in recent weeks, though, as last weekend's humbling 3-1 loss to newly-promoted Coventry City marked their fifth defeat from their last six Premier League games and extended their winless run in the division to seven.

Stadium of Light was also awash with boos on Thursday night, when Regis Le Bris's men went down 2-0 to Dinamo Zagreb in the Europa League, ending their unbeaten start in the tournament and leading to renewed sack talk.

The Sunderland hierarchy are not minded to remove Le Bris from his post just yet, though, and the Frenchman's focus now turns to repeating last season's shock 2-1 home and away wins against Chelsea, but not since 2001 have the Black Cats bested the Blues in three straight games.

Chelsea boss Alonso confirmed a triple fitness boost in his pre-game press conference, revealing that Emiliano Martinez is in contention to return from his jaw operation, while Aaron Anselmino and Jordan Henderson have battled back from injury and illness respectively.

The latter's presence may be crucial this weekend, as Moises Caicedo missed training earlier this week due to discomfort, and there are no guarantees that he will be fit to face the Black Cats.

Jorrel Hato (unknown), Maxence Lacroix (hamstring) Reece James (knee), Jamie Gittens (ankle) and Joao Pedro (quad) are confirmed absentees for Chelsea, whose playmaking star Cole Palmer will have a particular point to prove this weekend after being omitted from Thomas Tuchel's England squad yet again.

As for a jaded Sunderland side, Omar Alderete serves a one-game ban following his sending-off at Coventry, but Nordi Mukiele should exit concussion protocols in time to deputise for his fellow defender.

Daniel Ballard (hamstring), Habib Diarra (muscle) and Romaine Mundle (knee) will not return before the international break, though, while teenage striker Juan Riquelme Angulo is uncertain due to a contact injury.

Le Bris ripped up his second-string side in midweek, making no fewer than four half-time changes, so expect the likes of Trai Hume, Reinildo, Enzo Le Fee, Noah Sadiki and Brian Brobbey to return here.

Roefs; Hume, Mukiele, O'Nien, Reinildo; Xhaka, Sadiki; Rigg, Le Fee, Angulo; Brobbey

Penders; Acheampong, Fofana, Colwill, Palestra; Henderson, Lavia; Estevao, Palmer, Rogers; Neto

Fatigue should not play a significant role for Sunderland on Sunday given the alterations Le Bris made in midweek, but backing the Black Cats to get anything out of any Premier League game at present is a tough ask.

Therefore, even a Pedro-less Chelsea side - working on a full week's worth of rest - should stroll to victory, with an increasingly familiar clean sheet in tow.

Les Pirates picked up a comfortable success at Lorient last time out, whereas Les Gones have been busy on continental duty, sharing the spoils at Real Sociedad.

After a mediocre 12th-placed finish in Ligue 1 last season, Brest are aiming to qualify for European competition this time around, with their recent form suggesting that a continental charge could be successful.

Les Pirates have lost just one of their past four top-flight matches after picking up a 2-0 away triumph at Lorient on Monday night, when Ludovic Ajorque and Noah Edjouma found the net in the second half.

Aiming to record consecutive top-flight victories for the first time since early March, Brest are currently occupying 10th position in the Ligue 1 standings, eight points behind leaders Paris Saint-Germain.

Rather surprisingly, only four of Les Pirates' 12 league points have been collected at Stade Francis-Le Ble so far this campaign, with Julien Lachuer's men winning only one of their opening four home contests.

That sole success was impressive and emphatic in equal measure, though, as leading marksman Ajorque provided a goal and an assist in a 5-1 battering of relegation-threatened Angers on October 10.

Following back-to-back wins over Anderlecht and Conference League champions Crystal Palace to commence their Europa League campaign, Lyon have earned just one point from clashes with Hoffenheim (0-3) and Real Sociedad (1-1).

Les Gones are unbeaten across their past three encounters (W2 D1) with Brest; however, Les Pirates are unbeaten in the past three meetings (W2 D1) between the sides at Stade Francis-Le Ble.

Brest are expected to be without the services of Brendan Chardonnet, who is sidelined for up to two weeks because of a calf problem.

Les Pirates' options at centre-back are further reduced by the absence of 20-year-old Raphael Le Guen.

Wanted by Championship side Wrexham in the summer, Pavel Sulc is out until January with a knee injury.

#2018. Celtic star makes ‘terrified’ opposition claim after spearheading comeback

Celtic attacker Callum Osmand aims to build on the togetherness he felt at Parkhead on Thursday after experiencing both sides of the passion of supporters in four days.

Fans displayed their anger after Celtic’s 2-0 defeat at Falkirk on Sunday but the atmosphere was back to its best when Martin O’Neill’s side came from behind to beat Besiktas 3-2 in the Europa League.

Osmand sparked the comeback by scoring with his first touch after coming off the bench and later set up the first of fellow substitute Camilo Duran’s two goals.

Talking about the atmosphere, Osmand said: “You feel it, the crowd erupts and they really lift you. It’s incredible. When you’ve got Celtic Park like that, I feel for the opposition. They must be terrified because it lifts all of us and we’re so grateful for them.

“And the support when it gets like that is unmatched. It’s a great place to play and hopefully we can see more of those moments.”

Osmand had gone off at half-time at Falkirk but O’Neill’s triple substitution – with Duran and Colby Donovan also coming on – completed a major transformation in emotions.

“I completely understand what it means to people,” the 20-year-old said ahead of Sunday’s visit of Kilmarnock. “It’s a huge club and we want to be at the top and that’s what we strive to do.

“We know we need to be better at times, but I think it is just building off the good moments and learning from the bad and that’s all you can ask for. As long as we’re improving and getting better, that’s all you can really ask for.

“It is important to make sure everyone’s tight, especially when it’s going bad. That’s the main bit.

“Obviously, it’s a lot tougher for everyone when it’s not as good because the confidence, we might not be playing as forward as we should, and we all know that.

“But when the confidence comes and we’re just free-flowing, then everyone feels a lot better and we just need to keep building on it.”

Celtic face a Killie side who have conceded 28 goals in 12 William Hill Premiership games and whose manager, Neil McCann, has come under pressure from supporters.

McCann urged his players to show character in Glasgow on Sunday. “Every player has just got to be brave. You’ve got to continue to dig in.

“I’ve had so many occasions in my career where you could just hide, particularly on the wing when you’re getting battered and it’s not working for you. You’ve just got to keep taking the ball. It’s your job. You’ve got to keep being brave on it.

“If a manager wants you to play in a certain way and he’s given you the authority and the licence to go and continue to take it when you’re making mistakes, that’s the only way of coming through a difficult spot.

“And that’s where we’ve got to go to Celtic Park and really show our personality.”
